transcript.text: Had a new induction hob fitted by a mate last month. Tonight the big red cooker switch on the wall was hot to touch, there's a burning plastic smell and the hob keeps cutting out. What's going on?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A hot cooker switch with a burning plastic smell almost always means an electrical connection is overheating, and this needs a qualified electrician before the hob is used again. Please don't use it, even briefly, until it's been checked. What's most likely going on, in order: 1. A loose or badly tightened connection, either in the red cooker switch or at the outlet plate where the hob cable joins the wall. Induction hobs draw a lot of current, and a connection that isn't fully tight heats up, melts the plastic around it and can make the supply drop out, which would explain the hob cutting out. This is a common sign of an installation fault, and it often shows up a few weeks after fitting.
2. The supply isn't suited to the hob. Many induction hobs need a dedicated circuit with the right size of cable, switch and breaker. If the hob went onto an existing cooker circuit or a smaller cable, everything can run hot under load.
3. Less likely, a fault in the hob itself. Its own overheating protection can make it cut out, but that wouldn't normally make the wall switch hot or cause a burning smell at the switch. Safe things you can do now: 1. Switch the cooker circuit off at the consumer unit (fuse box), not just at the red switch, and leave it off. If the red switch or the plate looks damaged, don't touch it.
2. Once it's off and cooled, look at the front of the red switch and the hob's wall plate without opening them. Browning, melting or scorch marks would confirm overheating at that point. Seeing none doesn't mean it's safe, as the damage is often hidden behind the faceplate.
3. If it's easy to see, note the hob's power rating (on the rating plate or in the manual, in kW) and the number on the cooker circuit breaker (for example 32A or 40A). That helps the electrician quickly see whether the circuit suits the hob. If you see smoke or flames, or the smell gets stronger with the power off, get out and call 999. The next step is a qualified electrician (NICEIC or NAPIT registered) to check the switch, the connections and the circuit. Fitting a hob on its own circuit is notifiable work in England and Wales, so it's worth getting it properly certified at the same time. Once the supply side is confirmed sound, if the hob still cuts out we can look at the hob itself.

candidates: Loose or poorly made connection at the wall cooker switch or the hob's connection point, overheating under load (high)
Supply circuit not suited to the hob's load (cable, switch or breaker too small for an induction hob) (medium)
Fault inside the hob itself drawing abnormal current or overheating (low)

reading.symptom: cooker switch hot, burning plastic smell, hob cutting out

plan: They asked: "What's going on?" - answer that first.

Safety: a burning hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
The fault they reported is: "cooker switch hot, burning plastic smell, hob cutting out". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
